Core has no HTTP client, database or child-process dependency, and every extension crate depends only on core. **Differences users can observe**: (1) core knows no model provider, so a model *name* resolves through a default that the facade installs: the facade `Runner` (same five methods as the core one, kept in step by `scripts/check_runner_api.py`) registers the OpenAI provider on its first call, so `OPENAI_API_KEY` / `OPENAI_BASE_URL` still suffice, including for agents run through `Agent::as_tool`; a program that uses `opai_agents_core::Runner` directly, or builds without the `openai` feature, gets a `MissingProvider` error telling it to set `RunConfig.model_provider` or call `set_default_model_provider_factory`; (2) `default_model_provider()` is now `opai_agents::default_model_provider()` and exists only with the `openai` feature; (3) the OpenAI adapters are `opai_agents::openai::*` (was `opai_agents::model::openai::*`; the root re-exports `OpenAIProvider`, `CompatibleProvider`, `OpenAIChatCompletionsModel`, `OpenAIResponsesModel`, `DefaultOpenAiApi` and `get/set_default_openai_api` are unchanged); (4) `mcp` is no longer a default feature (`default = ["openai"]`), so `McpClient` and its transports need `features = ["mcp"]`, while the `McpServer` trait, `McpTool` and `mcp_function_tools` stay in core and always work with `Agent::mcp_servers`; (5) `opai_agents::testing` is a separate crate, always available; (6) `wire_events` (the Responses event emitter) and `replay_response` are public in core, for model implementors. Nothing about run behavior changed: the parity goldens, the request snapshots and the test counts are the same | Accepted |
| D-048 | `FunctionTool.needs_approval`, `ToolApprovalItem`, `RunState.approve` / `reject` | Approval is generalized into *resolution*, and the generic names are the primary ones. A tool call pauses before it runs when `FunctionTool.needs_resolution: NeedsResolution` says so (fixed, or per call from the arguments: `with_needs_resolution` / `with_needs_resolution_fn`), and is reported as a `ToolInterruptionItem` (`RunItem::ToolInterruption`). The host resolves it on the `RunState` with `resolve(item, ToolResolution)`: `Run` (Python: approve), `Reject { message }` (Python: reject), or `Output { output }`, which Python does not have: the tool is not run and the model receives `output` as the call's result, for work the host carried out elsewhere (e.g. a job that outlives the process; `provide_output(item, output)` is the shorthand). An output resolution goes through the same path as a rejection (no tool hooks, guardrails or timeout, since nothing runs), survives the JSON round trip, and reaches nested `Agent::as_tool` runs like an approval. Only the resolution names exist (the Python-name aliases `NeedsApproval`, `ToolApprovalItem`, `ApprovalDecision`, `ApprovalStore`, `with_needs_approval*` and `RunState::approval_status` were removed); the human-approval verbs `RunState::approve` / `reject` stay, and `#[function_tool(needs_approval)]` is still accepted next to `needs_resolution`. `McpServer::needs_resolution_for` returns the `NeedsResolution` of an MCP tool. **Breaking for Rust callers**: the fields `FunctionTool.needs_approval` and `AsToolConfig.needs_approval` are now `needs_resolution`, the enum variant `RunItem::ToolApproval` is `RunItem::ToolInterruption`, and `ToolResolution` has variants `Run` / `Reject` / `Output` instead of `Approved` / `Rejected`. Human-approval features built on top keep approval names: MCP `RequireApproval`, sticky `always_approve` / `always_reject` (`StickyDecision`), `DEFAULT_APPROVAL_REJECTION_MESSAGE`, `ToolErrorKind::ApprovalRejected`. RunState schema `/4` (D-012) | Accepted |
| D-049 | Responses stream that ends without a terminal event (`openai_responses.py` stream, `run_loop.py:2371`) | Python's adapter forwards the events it gets and does not synthesize anything; the Runner then raises `ModelBehaviorError("Model did not produce a final response!")` when no final response arrived. Rust (`crates/openai/src/responses.rs`, the `None` arm after the read loop) **tolerates** it: it builds the output from the `response.output_item.done` events seen, emits a synthesized `response.completed` continuing the sequence numbers, with zero usage, and logs a `warn!` (the reply may be truncated; a dropped connection looks the same). `response.failed` / `error` events still raise `ModelError::Behavior`. Reason: some OpenAI-compatible gateways never send `response.completed`; failing would make them unusable. Observable: a truncated reply is treated as a successful one and its usage reads 0 | Accepted. A strict switch (error instead of synthesize) may follow with the M2 capability matrix |

Verified to **match** Python in this audit: `AgentHooks.on_handoff(context, agent=new, source=old)`
is invoked on the *source* agent's hooks; output guardrails combine `RunConfig` + agent guardrails
and trip as `OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered`; `tool_choice` reset; `HandoffCallItem` /
`HandoffOutputItem` payload (`{"assistant": name}`); input guardrails run only on the first agent.

## Model retries (D-034)

`ModelSettings.retry` ports Python's runner-managed retries (`retry.py`, `run_internal/model_retry.py`),
and the Python behavior was checked against the vendored SDK scenario by scenario (backoff waits,
`Retry-After` precedence, exhausted budgets, stateful and replay-unsafe vetoes, `provider_suggested`,
`all` / `any`, the `conversation_locked` compatibility replay, usage accounting).

Ported: `ModelRetrySettings` (`max_retries`, `backoff`, `policy`; merged field by field in
`ModelSettings::resolve`, serialized without the policy), `ModelRetryBackoffSettings`, `RetryDecision`
(`approve_unsafe_replay`, delay, reason), `RetryPolicyContext`, `ModelRetryAdvice` /
`ModelRetryNormalizedError` / `ModelRetryAdviceRequest`, `retry_policies` (`never`, `provider_suggested`,
`network_error`, `retry_after`, `http_status`, `all`, `any`), per-attempt `ModelSettings.timeout`
(`ModelError::Timeout`, enforced by the runner for every `Model`, streamed or not), failed attempts
counted in `Usage` (zero-token `request_usage_entries`), the `conversation_locked` replay (3 times, 1s / 2s /
4s, disabled by `max_retries = 0`), and OpenAI advice (`x-should-retry`, 408 / 409 / 429 / 5xx, network
failures, `retry-after-ms` / `retry-after`).

Differences, all intentional:

| Area | Rust behavior | Reason |
|------|---------------|--------|
| Error type | HTTP failures are `ModelError::Status(ModelStatusError)` (status, headers, body), connection / timeout / body-read failures are `ModelError::Connection`; `Transport(String)` remains for undecodable bodies. The message text is unchanged. `ModelError` is now `Clone` | Retry policies need the status, headers and error code, which a string loses. Code that matched `ModelError::Transport` for an HTTP failure must match `Status` |
| Policies | Async closures returning `bool` or `RetryDecision` (`RetryPolicy::new`); built-ins are functions in `retry_policies` taking `Vec<RetryPolicy>` for `all` / `any` | No variadic arguments |
| Hidden client retries | None exist, so nothing is disabled between attempts | Python's OpenAI client retries by itself and the runner has to switch that off |
| Not ported | `replay_unsafe_request` (programmatic tool calling), `rewind` (no server conversation tracker), websocket retries, abort detection (cancelling a run drops the future, so there is no error to classify), `RetryPolicyContext.response_started` and the policy capability markers | No Rust counterpart |
| Streaming | A replay is blocked once an event other than `response.created` / `response.in_progress` reached the consumer, as in Python. The timeout covers a whole attempt (Python's covers waiting for each event) | The Rust adapters return the assembled response, so there is no per-event wait to time |
| `Retry-After` | Seconds, milliseconds (`retry-after-ms`) and the IMF-fixdate HTTP date; other date forms are ignored | No date parser dependency |
| Jitter | +-12.5% from a v4 UUID's random bits | No `rand` dependency |

## Streaming wire contract

`StreamEvent::RawResponse { data }` carries **one Responses API wire event** (Python:
`RawResponsesStreamEvent.data`, `stream_events.py:11-20`). Both OpenAI adapters and
`ScriptedModel` emit the same vocabulary, so a consumer never branches on the backend.

Which emitter does what:

| Emitter | Source | Python reference |
|---------|--------|------------------|
| `OpenAIResponsesModel` | provider SSE events, forwarded verbatim | `openai_responses.py:781` (`yield chunk`) |
| `OpenAIChatCompletionsModel` | synthesized from chat chunks | `chatcmpl_stream_handler.py` (15 event types) |
| `ScriptedModel` / default `Model::stream_response` | a finished response replayed | `testing/model.py` step expansion |

Rules the three share:

- **Vocabulary**: only `response.*` wire type names. No dialect names (the pre-D-011
  `output_text.delta` / `reasoning_text.delta` are gone).
- **Shape**: `item_id` / `output_index` / `content_index` / `summary_index` / `delta` /
  `logprobs` / `sequence_number`, matching the Python event objects. `item_id` is the item's own
  `id` (or `call_id`), falling back to `FAKE_RESPONSES_ID` (`"__fake_id__"`) when absent — which
  is the case for everything the Chat Completions adapter synthesizes, matching Python.
- **Ordering**: `response.created` → `output_item.added` → `content_part.added` → deltas →
  `*_done` → `output_item.done` → `response.completed`.
- **Numbering**: `sequence_number` is 0-based and monotonic (`chatcmpl_stream_handler.py:184`).
  Forwarded events keep the provider's number and are never renumbered; a synthesized terminal
  event continues from the last number seen.
- **`output_index`**: the reasoning item occupies 0, function calls take the next slots in
  arrival order, and the assistant message is assigned lazily right after the calls known when
  its first delta arrives (`_StreamOutputLayout`).
- **Terminal event**: `{"type":"response.completed","response":{…}}` with the full `response`
  object (`id`, `object`, `created_at`, `model`, `status`, `output`, `usage`, `tools`,
  `tool_choice`, `parallel_tool_calls`, `top_p`, `temperature`).

Deliberately not ported (see D-011): `response.output_text.annotation.added` is not synthesized
(`response.refusal.delta` / `.done` are, from Chat Completions `delta.refusal`, D-040), `logprobs` payloads are emitted as
`[]`. The per-event status per emitter is tabulated
in [COMPAT.md](./COMPAT.md#streaming-wire-events).

## Rust-only extensions

Capabilities Python does not have. They are not part of the parity comparison; the behavior they
extend still matches Python.

| ID | Addition | Behavior | Notes |
|----|----------|----------|-------|
| X-002 | `Runtime` (`crates/core/src/runtime.rs`) | The default model provider and the Tokio runtime behind blocking calls are owned by a `Runtime` value instead of process-wide statics: `Runtime::builder().provider(..).build()`, `runtime.set_model_provider(..)` / `set_model_provider_factory(..)`, and `Runtime::global()` for the old "one process-wide default" behavior. `set_default_model_provider_factory` stays as a thin wrapper over `Runtime::global()`, so existing callers and the facade `Runner`'s OpenAI installation are unchanged; the facade's extra `Once` guard is gone. Observable: two `Runtime`s can hold different providers in one process (mainly useful in tests, which previously had to serialize on a global) | Tracing's global switch/processor and the handoff history markers are still process-wide (`tracing`, `handoffs::history`); `Runtime::tracing_disabled` / `set_tracing_disabled` forward to them. Threading them through every `agent_span()` call site is a follow-up |
| X-001 | `Extensions` (D-014 follow-up, `docs/refactor/09-d1-context-generics.md`) | A run carries a type-keyed map of shared values next to Python's single `context`. `RunOptions::with(value)` adds one, `ctx.get::<T>()` / `ctx.require::<T>()` read it (`ToolContext::require` names the tool in its error). `RunOptions::context(value)` and `context::<T>()` / `try_context::<T>()` keep working and use the same map: the value is stored under its own concrete type. A second value of the same type replaces the first (a `warn!` in debug builds). Still not generic: type mistakes surface at run time | Declared requirements checked before the first turn: see X-004 |
| X-003 | `Tool` trait, `Tool::typed`, `ToolOutput` (`crates/core/src/tool/`) | Python only has the `FunctionTool` dataclass. Here `Tool` (`spec`/`policy`/`requires`/`call`) is a trait; `FunctionTool` is its concrete, SDK-owned implementation (`impl Tool for FunctionTool`). `FunctionTool::from_tool` adapts any `impl Tool` into one, so a hand-written tool runs through the exact same execution path as a built-in one — not a parallel code path. `FunctionTool::typed`/`typed_with_result` build the JSON Schema from a `Deserialize + JsonSchema` struct (what `#[function_tool]` generates for a function), for callers who want that without the macro. `ToolResult` is renamed `ToolOutput`; `interruptions`/`nested_state` are `pub(crate)` (not part of the public shape) — build one with `ToolOutput::output`/`::interrupted`, read it with `is_interrupted()`/`value()` | None |
| X-004 | `Tool::requires`, `TypeRequirement` (`crates/core/src/extensions.rs`, `run/agent_loop.rs`) | A tool declares the `Extensions` types it needs (`FunctionTool::require::<T>()`); `validate_tool_requirements` walks every agent reachable from the one the run starts with (including handoff targets) before the first model turn and fails with the agent, tool and type name when one is missing. Python has no such declaration — a missing value only ever surfaces as a `KeyError` inside the tool call. Calling `ctx.require::<T>()` without declaring it is still checked only at call time, same as today | `#[function_tool]` generating the declaration for a typed parameter is tracked for a later pass, not part of this change |
| X-005 | `ToolMiddleware`, `ModelMiddleware` (`crates/core/src/tool_middleware.rs`, `model_middleware.rs`) | Python has no equivalent; the closest are `tool_input_guardrails`/`tool_output_guardrails` (replace-or-reject only) and the single `call_model_input_filter`. `FunctionTool::with_middleware` wraps a tool's invocation onion-style (auth, rate limiting, audit, cache; can skip the call and return a cached `ToolOutput`). `ModelOptions::middleware` runs a list of `ModelMiddleware` after `call_model_input_filter`, in the order added, rewriting the request | Only request rewriting is covered; wrapping the model response/stream (metrics, caching) would reach into the retry/streaming call path and is not implemented yet |
| X-006 | Model-name effort suffix (`ReasoningEffort::split_model_name`, `run/resolve.rs`) | A model name resolved through a provider may end in `:<effort>` (`none`/`minimal`/`low`/`medium`/`high`/`xhigh`): `"o4-mini:high"` asks the provider for `o4-mini` and fills `reasoning.effort = high` unless the run or agent settings already choose an effort. Only those words are recognized, so tags like `llama3:8b` or `:free` pass through unchanged. Model *instances* are not affected | A real model whose name ends in `:high` etc. cannot be addressed by name; bind it as an instance instead |
| X-007 | `Capability`, `CapabilityParts` (`crates/core/src/agent/capability.rs`) | A named bundle of agent parts: tools, an instruction paragraph, input/output guardrails, default model settings and required extension types. `Agent::capability(..)` mounts it; the parts stay apart from the agent's own fields and are merged where they are read (tools after the agent's own and before MCP tools; instructions appended after a blank line; guardrails after the agent's own; model settings below the agent's, which are below the run's; requirements checked before the first turn), so builder order does not matter and mounting equals handing over the same parts by hand. An agent without capabilities behaves exactly as before | Hooks are not a part yet (an agent has one `hooks` slot; composing several needs a combinator). The built-in bundles (calculator, web fetch, file system, safe input/output, memory) arrive with the `tools` / `guardrails` / `sessions` crates |
| X-008 | `ModelProvider::get_model` is `async` (`crates/core/src/model/provider.rs`) | Python's `get_model` is synchronous. Here it is an `async fn` (via `async_trait`, re-exported as `opai_agents::async_trait`), so a provider can fetch credentials, refresh a token or look a deployment up without blocking the runtime. The runner awaits it once per turn that resolves a name, at the same point Python calls it. `CachedProvider` does not hold its lock across the await; concurrent misses may build twice but every caller gets the one instance stored first | Breaking for Rust implementors: add `#[async_trait]` and `async` to `get_model`, and `.await` direct calls |
| X-009 | `RunOptions::resolve_with`, `ToolResolver` (`crates/core/src/run/hitl.rs`) | Python returns every pause to the caller, who builds a `RunState`, approves or rejects and calls `Runner.run` again. With a resolver set, `Runner::run` / `run_state` / `run_blocking` ask the callback about each paused call (`ToolInterruptionItem` in, `ToolResolution` out: `Run`, `reject(msg)`, `output(value)`) and resume until the run finishes, using the same `RunState` resolution path, so nested `as_tool` pauses, `max_turns` and sessions behave exactly as in the explicit loop. Streamed runs fail with a `UserError` when a resolver is set rather than ignore it | In-process only: a run that must survive a restart still uses the explicit `RunState` JSON flow. Sticky `always_*` decisions are not available from the callback |
| X-010 | Resolution bound to its call (`ResolutionStore`, `run_state/resolutions.rs`) | Python keys an approval by call id only. Here `RunState::resolve` / `approve` / `reject` / `provide_output` also record the agent, tool and exact arguments of the paused call (`"bound"` in the state JSON), and the decision applies only to a call that matches all three; a call that does not match is treated as unresolved, so it pauses again (or follows a sticky decision) and logs a warning. Guarantees that what was approved is what runs, even if a stored state's arguments are edited. States without `bound` (written before this change) are applied by call id as before; a `bound` missing a field fails to load. `ResolutionStore::resolve(call_id, ..)` stays unbound | Editing arguments in a stored state is detected, but anyone who can edit the state can also edit `bound`; integrity of stored states (HMAC) comes with `RunStateStore` |
| X-011 | Agent-graph fingerprint in `RunState` (`agent_graph`, `RunState::allow_agent_graph_change`) | Python matches a resumed state to the agent by name only. A paused run here also records a fingerprint of the starting agent's graph (agent names, each agent's own and capability tool names, handoff tool names; sorted, so build order does not matter; MCP tools and `is_enabled` are left out), and `Runner::run_state` / `run_state_streamed` refuse a state whose fingerprint differs from the agent passed in, with a `UserError` that says how to proceed. `allow_agent_graph_change()` drops the check for a deliberate upgrade. States without `agent_graph` resume as before | A deploy that adds a tool to a paused agent needs `allow_agent_graph_change()` (or finishing old runs first) to resume them |
| X-012 | Guardrail [`Verdict`](crate::guardrail::Verdict) with severity (`error/payload.rs`, `guardrail.rs`) | Python's guardrail result is a single tripwire flag: a guardrail either lets the run continue or stops it. Here `GuardrailFunctionOutput` carries a `Verdict`: `Pass`, `Fail { reason, severity }` (stop; `Severity::High` and `Critical` also cancel the others still running in the same group, as Python cancels them on any tripwire) or `Transform(content)` (continue with rewritten content, e.g. redacted). `pass(..)` / `trip(..)` stay as the Python shapes. Only guardrails built with `run_in_parallel(false)` may transform the input (the model has already received it otherwise, and a parallel transform fails the run); two transforms of the same content fail the run instead of picking one. An input transform also replaces what the session stores, and the first turn's session flush waits for the blocking guardrails; an output transform replaces `final_output` only (the model's own message in `new_items` is left as written). Verdicts round-trip in a `RunState` (`verdict` next to `tripwire_triggered`) | The built-in guardrails (max length, PII, injection, keywords, schema) arrive with the `guardrails` crate |
| X-013 | Provider presets and a capability matrix (`opai-agents-providers`) | Python has no table of third-party servers: you build a `ModelProvider` yourself and register it. This crate ships one: base URL, key variable, protocol, capabilities and model prefixes for `openai`, `deepseek`, `gemini`, `groq`, `openrouter`, `anthropic` and `ollama`, plus endpoints declared with `AGENTS_PROVIDER_{N}_ENDPOINT` / `_API_KEY` / `_NAME` / `_DEFAULT_MODEL`. `ProviderRegistry::from_env()` registers every preset whose key is set; the router resolves `prefix/model` and infers an unprefixed name only when one brand owns it (`claude-*`, `deepseek-*`, `gemini-*`), never `llama3`/`qwen2.5`. `Capabilities` says what a provider supports and `UnsupportedCapability` names provider and capability instead of dropping a field. Endpoints must be `https` unless they are loopback or `AGENTS_PROVIDER_INSECURE_HTTP=1`; keys never appear in `Debug`, errors or traces | The table goes stale; `LAST_CHECKED` says when it was reviewed. Unknown model ids are always allowed through (private deployments). The guard checks what a request needs (reasoning, a JSON schema, tool calls, parallel calls, `store`, images, PDFs) and refuses what the provider lacks, as `ModelError::Unsupported`, and `Provider::build()` wraps every model it hands out so a single provider and one reached through the registry behave the same; it does not stream-check (`Streaming`, `StreamUsage`, `ResponsesApi` are properties of how the provider was built, and every adapter can stream or fall back), and there is no Anthropic native adapter |
| X-014 | Model catalogue and advice (`catalog.rs` of `opai-agents-providers`) | Python never looks at a model id: it sends what it is given. This crate keeps a small catalogue (only models whose history is settled) and says something when a request names one: `Retired` says it was retired and what to use instead, `Legacy` names the current one, and an id that is a near miss for a known one gets a "did you mean" suggestion. It is a hint, never a gate — an unknown id is always allowed through, because private deployments and gateways serve models no catalogue knows — and it reaches you as a `tracing::warn!` from the router | A catalogue is only as good as its last update; a missing model says nothing, and a model retired after `LAST_CHECKED` is not flagged |
| X-015 | Zero-configuration entry point (`opai_agents::run`, `AGENTS_OFFLINE`, the `providers` feature) | Python's quickstart still needs an `Agent` with a model and a configured client. Here `opai_agents::run(instructions, input)` builds the agent, discovers the provider from the environment (a preset whose key is set, `AGENTS_PROVIDER_{N}_ENDPOINT`, or the offline model when `AGENTS_OFFLINE=1`) and picks a model name (`AGENTS_MODEL` / `OPENAI_MODEL` / the provider's suggestion / `gpt-4o-mini`), so the same one line works before a key exists and after. `AGENTS_OFFLINE` wins over a key that is set, and its answer says it is offline. A local preset (Ollama) is registered only when its own variable (`OLLAMA_HOST`) says where it is, so a run with nothing configured fails with advice instead of guessing at localhost | Discovery happens per call, so a long-lived process that changes its environment needs to call `zero_config_options()` again; the offline model answers the same line whatever the input, which is not a simulation of a model |
| X-016 | `RunStateStore` (`core::memory::state_store`) | Python has no store for a paused run: you serialize the `RunState` yourself and decide where it lives. The trait (save / load / delete, with a TTL) is the contract the file, Redis and Postgres backends implement, plus `RunStateMigration` so a deployment can adapt states written by an older version, and `is_supported_schema` / `finish_load` so every backend migrates and version-checks the same way. A state that is present but unusable (unreadable schema, signature mismatch) is an error, never `None` | Only the trait is here; the backends come with `opai-agents-sessions`: `FileRunStateStore` (one state per file, atomic rewrite, cross-process lock), `RedisRunStateStore` (one key, TTL) and `PostgresRunStateStore` (one row, upsert). All three store the same envelope — signed with HMAC-SHA256 when `AGENTS_STATE_KEY` is set, compared in constant time, with the TTL and the migration hook — so integrity and expiry are decided once rather than per backend. Core ships no store of its own. Without a key the store still works but says so once per open | A signature only proves the state was written by someone with the key: whoever can write the file can also rewrite it together with its signature, so this is tamper detection, not tamper proofing |

| X-017 | `core::session_contract`, the shared `Session` contract, and `opai-agents-sessions` (`FileSession`) | Python has no shared test suite for session backends. This one runs the eight behaviours a backend must have — empty, order, `limit` takes the newest, `pop_item`, `replace_items`, a reader never sees a half-written history, `clear_session`, a 1 MiB item round trip — plus `assert_concurrent_writes` for the no-lost-update property. It is in core, not in `opai-agents-testing`, because an extension may not depend on another extension, which also means a backend outside this workspace can run it. Three backends ship with it and pass it: `FileSession` (JSONL, one item per line, locked across processes, rewritten atomically, session id validated: no separators, no leading dot, no symlink to follow), `RedisSession` (a list, `replace_items` in one MULTI, optional TTL) and `PostgresSession` (rows, `replace_items` in one transaction, every value bound and the table name checked before it reaches SQL). The two that talk to a server sit behind features and skip their tests when no server is configured | Concurrency is checked with 16 spawned writers, which is a property test and not a proof. `FileSession`'s file IO is blocking, as SQLite's is |

| X-018 | `opai-agents-observability`: batched export, sinks and metrics | Python's `add_trace_processor` takes any processor, and the ones people write (`BatchTraceProcessor` with a `TracingExporter`) do their file or HTTP IO on a task of their own; the SDK offers no queue, no bound and no drop policy, so a slow backend slows the run and a stuck one stops it. Here `BatchedProcessor` is the way to install an exporter: the callback — which runs inside the run loop — turns the span into JSON and `try_send`s it into a bounded `std::sync::mpsc` channel, and a thread of its own does the writing. A full queue drops the event and counts it (`dropped()`, warned on the first and every hundredth), because a run must never wait on its own telemetry; `force_flush` waits at most `FLUSH_TIMEOUT` (2 s) and warns instead of blocking. The writer is a thread and not a spawned task because writing is blocking IO and `force_flush` is synchronous: a task on a single-threaded runtime could not make progress while the caller parked. `ExportEvent` is a flat JSON shape (kind, `span_kind`, ids, name, timestamps, error, usage) that carries no request body, tool argument or model output, since the SDK's spans do not hold them. `ConsoleSink` and `JsonlSink` write it out today; `OtelSink` (`otel` feature) turns each ended span into an OpenTelemetry span through the tracer the application installed — OTLP included — depending on the API only, so no exporter, gRPC stack or runtime is pulled into a build that does not use it, and losing the SDK's ids on the way (the OTel API assigns its own), which is why `agents.span_id` / `agents.parent_id` carry them as attributes; `TracingSink` emits each event into the application's `tracing` subscriber under the target `opai_agents` (`DEBUG`; `WARN` for a failed span; `TRACE` for starts and trace events) — as events and not `tracing` spans, because the export runs on a writer thread where no span is entered, so the SDK's `span_id` / `parent_id` are fields; `Metrics` / `MetricsSink` count turns, tool failures, tokens and cost from the same stream, pricing usage with a `PriceTable` that leaves an unpriced model at zero rather than guessing | Telemetry that fails is lost: errors are logged and counted, never raised into the run, so only `dropped()` says they happened. Metrics are per process, not per trace, and a model missing from the price table contributes nothing to the cost |

| X-019 | Ready-made tools (`opai-agents-tools`) | Python ships hosted tools (web search, file search, computer use) that call OpenAI, and no local ones; a Python project writes its own tools, SSRF checks included, every time. This crate ships four local ones: `calculator` (a recursive-descent parser over numbers, `+ - * /`, parentheses and a unary minus — never an `eval`, so there is no way to reach a variable, a function or a file whatever the model writes), `clock` (the system time as one RFC 3339 string, with a fixed `+HH:MM` offset and never a zone database), `file_read` / `file_list` (one canonicalised root directory; `..`, absolute paths and symlinks that resolve outside it are refused, and a file over 1 MiB is refused rather than read) and `web_fetch` (`webfetch` feature), whose SSRF rule is checked in three places: an address written into the URL (decimal, hex, octal and short forms, IPv6, IPv4-mapped) is checked as the URL is read, on the first request and on every redirect hop; a name goes through a DNS resolver of its own, so every address a connection is about to use is checked; so loopback, link-local, private, multicast, reserved and unspecified ranges — the `9.`/`11.`/`21.`/`30.` blocks and carrier-grade `100.64/10` with them, in IPv6 and in IPv4-mapped form — are refused at connect time rather than before it, a redirect to another origin or down to `http` is refused unless asked for and a chain is capped at five hops; no system proxy is used (the check would be on the proxy's address, not the model's); and a response is read in pieces and cut off at 1 MiB, so a server that never stops sending cannot fill memory. Tests run a local server that counts connections and assert that a refused request made none | `web_fetch`'s check runs on the addresses its own resolver returns; a DNS server that lies for one lookup and tells the truth for the next is not covered, which is why `allow_private` is a deliberate switch and not a fallback. The tests cover the behaviour on a real socket; DNS rebinding between the resolver's answer and the connect is closed by the connection using the resolver's answer, not by a second lookup. `strip_tags` is a tag stripper, not an HTML parser: it removes `<...>` and collapses whitespace and does not decode entities |
| X-020 | Ready-made guardrails (`opai-agents-guardrails`) | Python has no built-in guardrails: each project writes its own, and the only answer a Python guardrail can give is "trip the run". Here a `Guard` is a check over text that says pass, fail or *rewrite*, and becomes an input or an output guardrail in one call (`.input()` is built `run_in_parallel(false)`, because a rewrite is only worth anything if the model never saw the original). Five ship: `MaxLength` (characters or bytes, per piece of text; a limit of zero is refused), `PiiRedactor` (emails, Luhn-valid card numbers, assignable-range SSNs and phone numbers → `[EMAIL]`/`[CARD]`/`[SSN]`/`[PHONE]`, redacting by default and refusing on request), `PromptInjection` (bounded phrase patterns for the usual instruction-override wordings, blind to zero-width characters and odd spacing), `BlockedKeywords` (literal, case-insensitive, whole-word by default so `skill` is not `kill`) and `SchemaValidator` (a subset of JSON Schema). A misconfiguration — an empty keyword list, a limit of zero, an unsupported schema keyword, a kind list with nothing in it — is a `BuildError` at construction, never a filter that silently does nothing. The matching is the `regex` crate's, linear in the text, and the tests feed it adversarial input. A failure says which rule and never quotes the text; the trace gets the guard's name and counts of strings checked and rewritten | `PiiRedactor` is pattern matching: it does not find names, addresses or numbers written out in words, and a bare ten-digit number is left alone because it is as likely an id; it is the second line, not the first. `PromptInjection` is a heuristic, not a boundary — an attack worded differently or in another language passes, and an article quoting an attack fails; the tests state both limits. `SchemaValidator` supports `type`, `enum`, `const`, `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties` (true/false), `items`, the length/size bounds and `minimum`/`maximum`; `$ref`, `oneOf`/`anyOf`/`allOf`, `pattern`, `not` and `if` are refused at construction because skipping one would accept what the schema means to refuse. Only one input guardrail may rewrite a given input (core's rule, X-012), so redaction and any other rewriter must be combined |
| X-021 | `CapabilityParts::deferred(description)`, tool `load_capability` (`crates/core/src/agent/deferred.rs`) | A capability marked deferred stays out of the prompt: the model sees one catalog line per unloaded capability (appended to the instructions) and a framework tool, `load_capability`, whose `name` argument is an enum of the unloaded names. Calling it makes the capability's tools and instructions visible from the next step; the tool disappears once nothing is left to load. Loading is per agent and per run, idempotent (a second load answers "already loaded"), and a name that is not a deferred capability of the agent loads nothing and is answered with the loadable names. Until loaded, the capability's tools are not offered and a call to one is an unknown-tool error like any other. Guardrails, model settings and `requires` apply from the start, so leaving a capability unloaded never bypasses a check. The loaded set lives in the run context and is saved in `RunState` (`loaded_capabilities`; states without it load with nothing loaded); on resume, the `load_capability` call that ran before the pause is matched to its saved output instead of being re-planned | Python has no on-demand tool loading. Loading takes effect on the next model step, not the current one. The `load_capability` name is reserved: a tool of the same name on the agent shadows it for the call lookup. Not part of the agent-graph fingerprint, since which capabilities are loaded is run state, not graph shape |
| X-022 | `RunOptions::runtime`, `Runtime::{set_trace_processors, add_trace_processor, flush_traces, set_tracing_disabled, set_conversation_history_wrappers, current}` | A run can execute on its own `Runtime`, which owns its default model provider, tracing switch and processors, and handoff history markers. The runtime travels in a task-local, read by `Runtime::current()` (the run's, else `Runtime::global()`); a trace or span ends on the runtime it started on. Two runs on two runtimes share no tracing or handoff state. The Python-named free functions (`set_trace_processors`, `set_tracing_disabled`, `set_conversation_history_wrappers`, …) keep acting on the global runtime | Python keeps these as process globals. A task spawned inside a run loses the runtime unless it is wrapped in `tracing::with_run_tracing_disabled` (the same rule as the run's tracing switch); an explicit `RunConfig.model.provider` still wins over the runtime's provider. `run_blocking` still uses the global runtime's thread pool |
| X-023 | `ToolSpec::new` / `ToolSpec::typed`, the `ToolPolicy` builders (`needs_resolution`, `enabled`, `timeout`, `timeout_behavior`, `on_failure`, `timeout_message`), `NeedsResolution::dynamic` | `Tool` is the extension point for a tool that is a component: state, typed arguments, a typed result, a declared dependency and a scheduling policy. For that to work outside the SDK, `ToolSpec` and `ToolPolicy` need constructors, since both are `#[non_exhaustive]`; before this they could only be built inside core, which made `impl Tool` impossible for a library consumer. `ToolSpec::typed::<Args>` builds the schema from the argument struct with the same conversion `FunctionTool::typed` uses, so the advertised schema and the `Deserialize` in `call` cannot drift apart | Python has no `Tool` trait; `FunctionTool` is a dataclass there. Covered by `examples/src/12_structured_tool.rs` and `crates/facade/tests/behavior_custom_tool.rs` |
| X-024 | `ToolMeta` / `TypedTool` traits, `#[derive(ToolMeta)]` with `#[tool(..)]`, `FunctionTool::from_typed` | Writing `impl Tool` by hand means repeating, in `spec`, `policy`, `requires` and `call`, what the argument struct already says. Here two types share the work: the `Args` struct gives the schema (`JsonSchema`, field doc comments become the descriptions) and the parse (`Deserialize`); the tool type, which may hold state, carries the identity, and the derive on it reads name, description (default: the tool type's doc comment), `timeout`, `requires(..)`, `needs_approval`, `needs_approval_if = path` (a `fn(&Args) -> bool` on the parsed arguments of each call) and `on_failure` (a format string with `{error}`). Unknown options are compile errors. The body is `TypedTool::run(&self, args, ctx)`, which returns a serializable result; `&self` is what lets a tool hold state (a client, a cache, a counter). Splitting tool from arguments also keeps the tool description out of the parameter schema: the advertised `parameters` carry no `title`, no repeated `description` and no unreferenced `$defs`. Same idea as nova's `ToolArgs` derive, built on `schemars` instead of its own schema writer | Python has no equivalent (`@function_tool` decorates a function). Covered by `crates/facade/tests/behavior_typed_tool.rs` and `examples/src/12_structured_tool.rs` |
| X-025 | `opai-agents-teams`, facade feature `teams` (`Team`, `TeamBuilder`, `TeamHandle`, `Role`, `TeamHooks`, `Budget`) | Python has no agent teams: handoffs swap the active agent and agents-as-tools nest a synchronous run, but nothing lets several long-lived agents work at once. This crate adds an actor layer on top of the core runner without touching core: each teammate is a task that sleeps on its mailbox, runs the role's agent when mail arrives, reports to the lead and sleeps again (an idle teammate makes no model calls). Teammates are created from `Role` templates registered by the application, so a lead cannot pick a model or widen tools. The caller's identity lives in the `TeamHandle` in `RunOptions` extensions, so senders cannot be forged. Messages are injected between runs and quoted as untrusted data. The task list claims atomically and resolves dependencies. Shutdown is cooperative with a cancellation fallback; a panicking teammate is isolated and its tasks are released. Tool calls and plans that need a decision bubble up to the lead through the existing resolution mechanism. In-process only: `Mailbox` and `TaskBoard` are traits so a durable store can follow | Design in `docs/AGENT-TEAMS.md`. Covered by `crates/teams/tests` and `examples/src/23_teams.rs` |
| X-026 | MCP protocol 2026-07-28 in `opai-agents-mcp` | Python speaks the `initialize` handshake only. This client first sends `server/discover`; a server that lists `2026-07-28` is used statelessly (version, capabilities and client info in every request's `_meta`; `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` headers on HTTP; `ttlMs` of a tool list honoured), and any other answer falls back to `initialize`, so servers deployed today are unaffected. A `resultType: "input_required"` reply (multi round-trip requests) is an error, since the client declares no capability to answer it. Not implemented: `subscriptions/listen`, the tasks extension, `x-mcp-header`, `cacheScope`. Covered by `crates/mcp` unit tests and `crates/facade/tests/mcp_interop.rs` (old-dialect server). | Accepted |

## How to add an entry

1. Assign the next `D-NNN` ID. Older `B*` / `D-A..D-N` IDs are kept as they are because code,
   tests and commits refer to them; they are not renumbered.
2. Cite the Python path (file + symbol) under `vendor/openai-agents-python` @ `v0.23.1`.
3. State the Rust behavior and whether callers can observe the difference.
4. Mark the align plan: `Document only` / `Accepted` / `Gap` / `Later phase` / `Bug (fix)`.

---

# Source: docs/MIGRATION-FROM-PYTHON.md

# Migrating from openai-agents-python

For someone who knows the Python SDK (@ `v0.23.1`) and wants the same thing in Rust. It lists
what maps directly, what changes shape, and — the part that actually costs time — **what you have
to write yourself**.

The full support matrix is [COMPAT.md](./COMPAT.md); the reasoning behind each difference is
[DEVIATIONS.md](./DEVIATIONS.md).

## 1. What maps almost one-to-one

| Python | Rust |
|--------|------|
| `Agent(name=..., instructions=..., tools=..., handoffs=..., model=..., model_settings=..., output_type=..., hooks=...)` | `Agent::new(name).instructions(..).tools(..).handoffs(..).model(..).model_settings(..).output_type(..).hooks(..)` |
| `Runner.run(agent, input)` | `Runner::run(&agent, input, RunOptions::default()).await` |
| `Runner.run_sync(...)` | `Runner::run_blocking(&agent, input, RunOptions::default())` (D-001) |
| `Runner.run_streamed(...)` + `async for` | `Runner::run_streamed(agent, input, opts)` + `next_event().await` |
| `@function_tool` | `#[function_tool]` (schema from Rust types, doc comment = description; D-002) |
| `handoff(agent)` / `handoff(agent, tool_name_override=...)` | `handoff(agent)` / `handoff_with(agent, name, description)` |
| `input_guardrails` / `output_guardrails` | `input_guardrail(name, fn)` / `output_guardrail(name, fn)`, returning a `GuardrailFunctionOutput` (`Verdict`: pass, fail, transform) |
| `RunHooks` / `AgentHooks` subclasses | `impl RunHooks` / `impl AgentHooks` (every method has a no-op default) |
| `SQLiteSession` | `SqliteSession` (feature `sqlite`; **the same database file works in both SDKs**, D-038) |
| `RunConfig(...)` / `RunOptions(...)` | `RunConfig::default()` plus grouped fields or chain methods, see [RunConfig groups](#runconfig-groups). `RunConfig` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so a struct literal does not compile outside the crate |
| `ModelSettings(...)` | `ModelSettings { .. }` (22 fields; 3 OpenAI-only ones are not ported, D-017) |
| `Runner.run(agent, state)` after HITL | `Runner::run_state(&agent, state, opts)` |
| `ScriptedModel` / `ModelStep` | `ScriptedModel` / `ModelStep` in `opai_agents::testing` |

## 2. Differences you will hit on day one

| Python | Rust | Why |
|--------|------|-----|
| `RunContextWrapper[TContext]`, generic over the context | `RunContextWrapper` carrying `Arc<dyn Any>`; `context::<T>()` / `try_context::<T>()` | No generic parameter threaded through `Agent` / `Runner` (D-014). Type errors surface at runtime with an explicit message |
| `Agent` is mutable, `agent.tools.append(t)` | `Agent` is a plain cloneable value; `Agent::new(..).tools(vec![..])` | Owned graph (D-030) |
| Cyclic handoffs: build, then mutate `handoffs` | `handoff_to_name("A")` — a late-bound handoff resolved by name at run time | Rust cannot build a cyclic owned graph (D-030) |
| `max_turns=10` default; `None` disables | same: `RunOptions::default()` is `Some(10)`, `None` disables the limit | D-042 |
| Exceptions (`MaxTurnsExceeded`, `ModelBehaviorError`, …) | `AgentsError` enum (`AgentsError::MaxTurns(..)`, `AgentsError::Model(ModelError::Behavior(..))`) | Rust has no exception hierarchy |
| `failure_error_function=None` raises | `FunctionTool::raise_on_error()` | B7 |
| Default API is Responses | Default is **Chat Completions**; opt into Responses with `set_default_openai_api(Responses)` or the `openai_responses/<model>` prefix | D-I: nearly every compatible server speaks Chat Completions |
| `AsyncOpenAI` client passed around | `OpenAIProvider::from_env()` / `CompatibleProvider::new(base_url)`; `MultiProvider` for `prefix/model` routing | D-013 |
| Tool returns `str` or a structured output part | Tool returns one `serde_json::Value`, rendered as text | D-044: images / files cannot be handed back to the model |
| `Agent.as_tool(...)` with ~18 keywords | `AsToolConfig { name, description, needs_resolution, max_turns }` | D-043 |
| `enable_verbose_stdout_logging()` | the `tracing` crate | — |

## 3. What you must write yourself

This is the real cost of migrating, and it is why the README's positioning section exists.

| You want | Python gives you | In Rust you write |
|----------|------------------|-------------------|
| Web search, file search, code interpreter, image generation | `WebSearchTool`, `FileSearchTool`, `CodeInterpreterTool`, `ImageGenerationTool` | A `FunctionTool` (or an MCP server) that calls the API you want |
| Remote MCP through OpenAI | `HostedMCPTool` | `McpClient::streamable_http(..)` — your SDK talks to the server instead of OpenAI |
| Shell commands | `ShellTool` / `LocalShellTool` | A `FunctionTool` that runs `tokio::process::Command`. **Do your own sandboxing** |
| File edits | `ApplyPatchTool` + `apply_diff` | A `FunctionTool` over your own patch application |
| Computer use | `ComputerTool` + `Computer` | A `FunctionTool` driving your own automation |
| Trace export to a backend | `add_trace_processor(BatchTraceProcessor(...))`, `set_tracing_export_api_key` | `impl TracingProcessor` for OTLP / Langfuse / whatever you use. Cloud export is not planned (D-004) |
| Long-context handling via the API | `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` (`responses.compact`) | `CompactingSession` + `ModelSummarizer` (any model), or `ContextWindowTrimmer` / `ToolOutputTrimmer` as a `call_model_input_filter`. Provider-neutral, and not OpenAI-only (D-039) |
| Redis / MongoDB / SQLAlchemy session storage | `agents.extensions.memory.*` | `impl Session` |
| Realtime / voice | `agents.realtime`, `agents.voice` | Not available |
| A sandboxed execution runtime | `agents.sandbox` | Not available; isolate at the process/container level |

## 4. Things that are better here

Not a migration aid, but worth knowing before you decide it is a downgrade:

- `run_blocking` / `run_blocking_on` work from any thread, with or without a runtime (D-001).
- `CancelMode::{Immediate, AfterTurn}` and `cancel_on_drop(true)` — Python's `cancel()` has no
  "let the turn finish" mode (D-031).
- `CompatibleProvider`: a base URL with an optional key, for vLLM / Ollama / LiteLLM / gateways.
- The Chat Completions adapter tolerates non-conforming servers (missing tool-call ids, list
  `content`, error chunks) and replays DeepSeek reasoning / Gemini thought signatures /
  Claude thinking blocks (D-040).
- `ensure_strict_json_schema` has depth and node budgets, so a hostile or pathological schema
  cannot blow up the process.
- The stdio MCP client clears the child's environment down to a safe allow-list instead of
  inheriting your API keys (D-041).
- `RunOptions::resolve_with(|call| async { .. })`: Python returns every pause to you; here a
  callback resolves the paused calls and the run resumes by itself, and the explicit `RunState`
  flow is still there when the run has to outlive the process (X-009).
- A resolution given through `RunState` is bound to the agent, tool and arguments of the call it
  answered: an approval cannot be carried to a call whose arguments changed, even in a stored
  state (X-010). Resuming also checks a fingerprint of the agent graph (X-011).
- A guardrail returns a `Verdict`: pass, fail (with a reason and a severity) or
  `Transform(content)`, so it can redact and let the run continue instead of only stopping it
  (X-012).
- `FunctionTool::typed`: one `#[derive(Deserialize, JsonSchema)]` struct gives you the tool's
  schema and its parsed arguments, so a tool needs no hand-written JSON.
- `Capability`: a named bundle of tools, instructions, guardrails and model settings you mount on
  an agent, equal to handing over its parts by hand (X-007).
- `ModelProvider::get_model` is `async`, so a provider can fetch credentials or look a deployment
  up before it builds the model (X-008).

## RunConfig groups

Python's `RunConfig` is one flat dataclass; here its fields are grouped by topic. Each group is a
`#[non_exhaustive]` struct with chain methods, and `RunConfig` has `with_model` / `with_tracing` /
`with_session` / `with_handoff` / `with_tools`. In practice you rarely touch `RunConfig` at all:
`RunOptions` chains the common ones (`model`, `temperature`, `max_turns`, `reasoning`, `session`,
`hooks`, `workflow_name`, `context`, `resolve_with`, `with`) and hands you a closure for each group
(`.tracing(..)`, `.tools(..)`, `.session_opts(..)`, `.config(..)`).

| Python `RunConfig` field | Rust |
| --- | --- |
| `model` | `config.model.model_ref` (chain: `ModelOptions::model(..)`) |
| `model_provider` | `config.model.provider` |
| `model_settings` | `config.model.settings` |
| `reasoning_item_id_policy` | `config.model.reasoning_item_id_policy` |
| `call_model_input_filter` | `config.model.input_filter` (chain: `ModelOptions::input_filter(..)`) |
| `tracing_disabled` | `config.tracing.disabled` |
| `workflow_name`, `trace_id`, `group_id` | `config.tracing.workflow_name`, `.trace_id`, `.group_id` |
| `trace_metadata` | `config.tracing.metadata` |
| `trace_include_sensitive_data` | `config.tracing.include_sensitive_data` |
| `tracing` | `config.tracing.config` |
| `session_input_callback`, `session_settings` | `config.session.input_callback`, `.settings` |
| `nest_handoff_history`, `handoff_history_mapper`, `handoff_input_filter` | `config.handoff.nest_history`, `.history_mapper`, `.input_filter` |
| `tool_not_found_behavior`, `tool_execution`, `tool_name_collision_policy` | `config.tools.not_found_behavior`, `.execution`, `.name_collision_policy` |
| `tool_error_formatter`, `output_guardrail_blocked_message` | `config.tools.error_formatter`, `.guardrail_blocked_message` |
| `input_guardrails`, `output_guardrails` | `config.input_guardrails`, `config.output_guardrails` |

```rust
let options = RunOptions::new()
    .with(tenant)
    .temperature(0.2)
    .workflow_name("support")
    .tools(|t| *t = t.clone().not_found_behavior(ToolNotFoundBehavior::ReturnErrorToModel));
```

# Source: docs/COMPARISON.md

# How this SDK compares

Two Rust neighbours: [Rig](https://github.com/0xPlaygrounds/rig) and
[ADK-Rust](https://github.com/zavora-ai/adk-rust). And the Python SDK this one ports.

The rows about this SDK come from this repository's code and tests. The rows about the other two come
from their public documentation at the time of writing and are deliberately coarse — both move fast,
so check their docs before relying on a cell.

| | This SDK | [openai-agents-python](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python) | Rig | ADK-Rust |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Starting point | port of v0.23.1, pinned in `vendor/PINNED_VERSION` | the reference implementation | independent framework | a Rust agent development kit in the style of Google's ADK |
| Behaviour checked against a reference implementation | yes: 13 declarative scenarios run through both implementations (`conformance/`) | — | no shared oracle | follows ADK's model, no shared oracle |
| Scope | the Python SDK's agent loop, provider-neutral | hosted OpenAI features included | provider abstraction, agents, RAG with 10+ vector stores, WASM | agents, workflow and graph agents, realtime voice, RAG, A2A servers |
| Extensibility | one trait each: `Tool`, `Model`, `ModelProvider`, `Session`, `TracingProcessor`, `Capability` | same set, Python protocols | `Tool` trait, provider traits, hooks | `Agent` trait, `#[tool]` macro, callbacks |
| Tool arguments | `#[function_tool]` or `FunctionTool::typed` from one `schemars` struct | `@function_tool` from type hints | `Tool` trait with JSON Schema | `#[tool]` macro with `schemars` |
| Business context | typed values in an `Extensions` map, a missing one reported with its type name | `RunContext` with any user object | agent state | session state |
| Pausing for approval | `needs_resolution` + `RunState` JSON + `resolve_with` closure | `needs_approval` + `RunState` | own state machine | graph interrupts, HITL |
| Guardrail verdicts | `Pass`, `Fail`, **`Transform`** (a rewrite is a result, not a refusal) | tripwire only | — | callbacks and guardrails |
| Provider presets | a table with a capability matrix that refuses rather than degrades silently | OpenAI plus compatible endpoints | 20+ providers, feature-gated | 14+ providers, feature-gated |
| On-demand tool loading | `CapabilityParts::deferred` | — | — | — |
| Scaffolding | `cargo opai new`, 3 templates | — | examples, no scaffolding CLI | `cargo adk new`, 13 templates, 9 addons, 5 enterprise patterns |
| Offline development | `AGENTS_OFFLINE=1` | `ScriptedModel` in tests | cassette record/replay | provider-dependent |

## Where this SDK is weaker, on purpose

Being honest about the trade: Rig has a far wider integration surface (20+ providers, 10+ vector
stores as companion crates, an onchain kit, `wasm32-unknown-unknown` support). ADK-Rust has a much
larger feature set (realtime voice, graph workflows with checkpointing and human-in-the-loop
interrupts, RAG with six vector-store backends, A2A servers, declarative tool scopes, a runtime UI)
and a far more developed scaffolding CLI.

This SDK deliberately skipped all of that. `docs/IMPROVEMENT-PLAN.md` lists the non-goals: hosted
OpenAI tools, real-time voice, RAG and vector stores, a visual studio. What it spends its complexity
on instead is *behavioural fidelity* — a Python oracle it can be diffed against — plus the parts a
Rust SDK can do better than a Python one: construction-time validation, `#[non_exhaustive]` everywhere
before the first release, and a `Transform` verdict that redacts instead of refusing.

## What is different from Python on purpose

`docs/DEVIATIONS.md` is the authoritative list, with an id per row (`D-…` for behaviour differences,
`X-…` for Rust-only additions). The ones worth knowing before choosing this SDK:

- **No hosted OpenAI tools.** Web search, file search, code interpreter, image generation, hosted
  MCP, computer use, `Agent.prompt` and the Conversations API are out of scope: they exist only
  because OpenAI hosts them. Anything that needs only a compatible *protocol* is in scope.
- **`RunState` is not Python's wire format.** The JSON schema is `openai-agents-rs/4`; use one
  language per durable state store.
- **Additions with no Python counterpart**: `Capability` bundles and `deferred` loading,
  `Verdict::Transform`, the provider presets, the ready-made tools and guardrails, `opai_agents::run`.
  They are registered under "extensions" in `docs/DEVIATIONS.md` and kept out of the parity
  comparison, so the behaviour alignment stays a clean check.

## Choosing

- Coming from the Python SDK, or depending on its exact behaviour: this SDK — then read
  `docs/MIGRATION-FROM-PYTHON.md`.
- Wanting the widest provider and vector-store coverage, or WASM: Rig.
- Wanting voice, graph workflows, A2A, a runtime UI, and a template for each: ADK-Rust.
- Wanting an agent loop whose behaviour you can diff against a reference implementation: this is the
  only one of the three that can do that.

---

# Source: STABILITY.md

# Stability

`0.1.0` of every crate is on crates.io; `0.2.0` is the next release. While the version is `0.x`, a minor release may still change
a public item; this file says what level each crate is at and how change is handled.

## Levels

| Level | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Unstable** | May change or disappear in any release. Behind a Cargo feature or documented as experimental. |
| **Stabilising** | The shape is settled and being reviewed. A change needs a changelog entry and a migration note. |
| **Stable** | Changes only in a major version (or a minor one while the version is `0.x`), with at least one release of deprecation first. |

## Crates

| Crate | Level now | Planned |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `opai-agents-core` | Unstable | Stabilising. Public enums and structs become `#[non_exhaustive]` in 0.2.0. |
| `opai-agents-openai` | Unstable | Stabilising |
| `opai-agents` (facade) | Unstable | Stabilising |
| `opai-agents-macros` | Unstable | Stabilising |
| `opai-agents-mcp` | Unstable | Unstable |
| `opai-agents-providers` | Unstable | Unstable |
| `opai-agents-sessions` | Unstable | Unstable |
| `opai-agents-observability` | Unstable | Unstable |
| `opai-agents-tools` | Unstable | Unstable |
| `opai-agents-guardrails` | Unstable | Unstable |
| `opai-agents-teams` | Unstable | Unstable |
| `opai-agents-testing` | Unstable | Unstable |

## Behaviour versus API

Run semantics follow the pinned Python SDK (`vendor/PINNED_VERSION`) and are checked by the
conformance scenarios. The Rust API shape is allowed to differ from Python's; every difference is
listed in `docs/DEVIATIONS.md`.

## Serialized data

`RunState` carries a schema id (`openai-agents-rs/4` today). Older ids keep loading; a new id is
introduced only with a changelog entry. A paused run is resumed by the SDK version that wrote it or a
newer one, never an older one.

## Deprecation

Once a crate is Stabilising or Stable, an item is marked `#[deprecated(note = "use X")]` for at
least one release before removal, and the changelog lists it under **Deprecated** and later
**Removed**.

## Minimum Rust version

`rust-version` is `1.89`, checked by the `msrv` job in CI on every push: the published crates must
compile with that compiler, tests included. The floor is set by the dependencies (`uuid` needs 1.89;
1.88 fails to build it), not by the SDK's own code. One exception: the `postgres` feature needs
**1.94**, because `sqlx` 0.9 declares it and Cargo refuses it on anything older; every other
feature builds on 1.89. The project itself is developed and linted with
`1.99` (`rust-toolchain.toml`), so a newer standard-library API can slip in; the `msrv` job is what
catches it. Raising `rust-version` is a breaking change and goes in the changelog.
